title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. And most importantly... the Footstrs were still in his shoes. Every day. That mattered. Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag. WEEK 3 One night I noticed something strange. The ice pack was still in the freezer. Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic. That week... I hadn't. title: Every soccer-mom needs to see this ☝️
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. And most importantly... the Footstrs were still in his shoes. Every day. That mattered. Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag. Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it. I simply hadn't thought about it. Neither had my son. Again... nothing dramatic. No miracle. Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine... that suddenly wasn't happening as often. WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT I got curious. Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on. So I asked my son: “Try your customs again.” He rolled his eyes. Eventually agreed. I put them into his shoes. He pushed his foot down... stopped... and immediately said: “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them. Then I looked. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. And I want to say this again because it's important: The custom orthotics did work when he wore them. That's not why I stopped using them. I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare. Appointments. Fittings. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. A rigid device my kid hated. And then... just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance... his feet were already too big. I did not want to start all over again. That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”... and started looking practical. Four pairs for $30. Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device. And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day. One pair in his school shoes. One in his sneakers. One in his soccer cleats. One for another pair he wears regularly. That is a completely different decision from: “Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?” THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard. There were three things that made sense. 1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad. There is structure underneath the arch. When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse. But it still flexes with the foot. Walking. Running. Cutting. Playing. The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape. It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving. 2 - HEEL CUSHIONING Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact. Sprint. Stop. Jump. Land. Sprint again. Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel. So there's comfort where the foot lands... and structure where it needs support. 3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES This was the other big reason I liked them. I didn't want our long-term plan to be: “Put something in his shoe forever and hope.” The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs. The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. That made much more sense to me. WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK The pharmacy inserts? Easy to wear. Not enough structure for what I wanted. The custom orthotics? Plenty of structure. Expensive. Rigid. A whole specialist process. Quickly outgrown. And most importantly... my kid wouldn't consistently wear them. Footstr landed in the middle. More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried. More flexible than the customs he'd rejected. Cushioning under the heel. Support under the arch. Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer. And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous. WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED First time they put them on: Don't expect fireworks. Honestly, the best answer might be: “They're comfortable.” Or: “They're fine.” That's a win. You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe. First practice: This is the first real test. Cleats tightened. Feet getting hot. Running. Jumping. Cutting. See whether your kid actually keeps them in. That's what mattered most to me. First week: Watch the ordinary things. Are they still wearing them? Are you fighting about them before practice? Are they pulling them out halfway through? What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints? Over the next few weeks: Keep your expectations realistic. Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight. It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them... while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow. IF YOU JUST ORDERED... Don't panic like I did. When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear. A few weeks later... I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown... while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats. That comparison pretty much answered the question for me. IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET... If your kid's feet roll inward... Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports... Or you've already been through the nightmare of expensive custom orthotics they won't consistently wear... Footstr gives you a much simpler place to start. Flexible arch support. Heel cushioning. A strengthening program. And support designed around active, growing feet without locking them against something hard and rigid. Right now, you can get four pairs for $30. So instead of constantly moving one pair between shoes, you can keep them where your kid actually needs them. School shoes. Sneakers. Cleats. Sports shoes. For me? That was a much easier decision than: Another specialist appointment. Another fitting. Another wait. Another $400 custom orthotic. title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. And most importantly... the Footstrs were still in his shoes. Every day. That mattered. Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag. WEEK 3 One night I noticed something strange. The ice pack was still in the freezer. Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic. That week... I hadn't. Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it. I simply hadn't thought about it. Neither had my son. Again... nothing dramatic. No miracle. Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine... that suddenly wasn't happening as often. WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT I got curious. Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on. So I asked my son: “Try your customs again.” He rolled his eyes. Eventually agreed. I put them into his shoes. He pushed his foot down... stopped... and immediately said: “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them. Then I looked. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. And I want to say this again because it's important: The custom orthotics did work when he wore them. That's not why I stopped using them. I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare. Appointments. Fittings. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. A rigid device my kid hated. And then... just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance... his feet were already too big. I did not want to start all over again. That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”... and started looking practical. Four pairs for $30. Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device. And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day. One pair in his school shoes. One in his sneakers. One in his soccer cleats. One for another pair he wears regularly. That is a completely different decision from: “Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?” THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard. There were three things that made sense. 1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad. There is structure underneath the arch. When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse. But it still flexes with the foot. Walking. Running. Cutting. Playing. The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape. It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving. 2 - HEEL CUSHIONING Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact. Sprint. Stop. Jump. Land. Sprint again. Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel. So there's comfort where the foot lands... and structure where it needs support. 3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES This was the other big reason I liked them. I didn't want our long-term plan to be: “Put something in his shoe forever and hope.” The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs. The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. That made much more sense to me. WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK The pharmacy inserts? Easy to wear. Not enough structure for what I wanted. The custom orthotics? Plenty of structure. Expensive. Rigid. A whole specialist process. Quickly outgrown. And most importantly... my kid wouldn't consistently wear them. Footstr landed in the middle. More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried. More flexible than the customs he'd rejected. Cushioning under the heel. Support under the arch. Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer. And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous. WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED First time they put them on: Don't expect fireworks. Honestly, the best answer might be: “They're comfortable.” Or: “They're fine.” That's a win. You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe. First practice: This is the first real test. Cleats tightened. Feet getting hot. Running. Jumping. Cutting. See whether your kid actually keeps them in. That's what mattered most to me. First week: Watch the ordinary things. Are they still wearing them? Are you fighting about them before practice? Are they pulling them out halfway through? What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints? Over the next few weeks: Keep your expectations realistic. Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight. It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them... while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow. IF YOU JUST ORDERED... Don't panic like I did. When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear. A few weeks later... I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown... while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats. That comparison pretty much answered the question for me. IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET... If your kid's feet roll inward... Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports... Or you've already been through the nightmare of expensive custom orthotics they won't consistently wear... Footstr gives you a much simpler place to start. Flexible arch support. Heel cushioning. A strengthening program. And support designed around active, growing feet without locking them against something hard and rigid. Right now, you can get four pairs for $30. So instead of constantly moving one pair between shoes, you can keep them where your kid actually needs them. School shoes. Sneakers. Cleats. Sports shoes. For me? That was a much easier decision than: Another specialist appointment. Another fitting. Another wait. Another $400 custom orthotic. And another argument with my kid about whether he'd actually wear it. Click below to see the Footstr InsoleX 👇 https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

title: The Amazon Explains Why Your Feet Hurt
body: Researchers filmed people in the Amazon walking barefoot. Not one of their steps looked the same. Yours have looked the same for years… Not genetics. Not special feet. Their feet feel the ground, and that feeling tells their muscles when to fire. On the trail, in the forest, every landing is different. Foam cut that feeling off about 50 years ago. Now your feet are numb. Every step lands the same, the pressure piles up in the same spots, and the arch drops because the muscles never get the signal to hold it. Knees compensate. Hips compensate. Back compensates. That's why you hurt everywhere, and why nothing has stuck. Orthotics propped your feet up until the muscles forgot how. PT woke them for an hour, then the same numb shoes put them back to sleep. Barefoot shoes took the cushion away and gave your feet nothing to feel. All of them worked around the problem. None of them taught your feet to work. Introducing SuperSocks WoodCarved 2.0. The one and only sock on the market with a patented sole, hand-sewn to your exact pressure points to reactivate your foot muscles. Biomechanics specialists mapped the exact points where a bare foot needs to feel pressure to make its muscles fire. We built those points into the sole. Pressure-Mapped Activation. Each full-grain cowhide section is hand-stitched right where your foot needs it, so: ✅ Every section tells the muscle under it to fire, every step ✅ It's stitched, so it never slips off its spot ✅ Your feet feel the ground again, and your knees and back stop taking the hit Full-grain is the top layer of the hide, so the section that works hardest doesn't wear through. Dyneema® knit around it, the same fiber in cut-resistant gear. Within days your feet start waking up. Keep wearing them and the walks you gave up come back. 🔄 30-Day Money-Back Guarantee Give your feet back the feeling that makes them work.

title: Best Shoes for Plantar Fasciitis
body: If you've got plantar fasciitis, stop wearing shoes that fold in half. Soft and bendy feels comfortable in the shop... but it overloads your arch all day. Here are the 5 features I look for when helping patients recover: 1️⃣ Firm heel counter You want the back of the shoe to feel solid. This limits excessive pronation and keeps the ankle stable. 2️⃣ Deep, supportive heel cup It should wrap around your heel bone and spread pressure evenly. This reduces strain through the inside of the heel. @kurufootwear builds this directly into the shoe with their curved heel technology, so you can actually feel that medial heel support. 3️⃣ Higher heel to toe drop A thicker heel compared to the forefoot reduces strain on your calf, arch, and plantar fascia. 4️⃣ Stiffness through the midfoot If you can easily twist or fold the shoe, it is too soft. A firmer shoe gives your foot the stability it needs while healing. 5️⃣ Slight rocker This helps roll you forward so you are not overloading your big toe and arch with every step. The right shoe will not cure plantar fasciitis overnight... but the wrong shoe will slow your recovery down. Check out @kurufootwear's range of shoes. #ad

brand: Tana Amen, BSN, RN with Orthofeet
body: I spent years thinking my back was the problem. After my injury, I learned something that changed the way I think about movement forever: your body works as one connected system. When your feet aren’t properly supported, your ankles, knees, hips, pelvis, and even your lower back can end up compensating. I can’t change my scoliosis or the injuries I’ve had, but I can choose the things that help me move with less pain and keep doing the things I love. That’s why I’ve been wearing @orthofeet_us. They give me the support and shock absorption I need, and yes, they’re actually cute too. Because if they weren’t... I’d probably still be searching. #OrthofeetPartner #HealthyAging #HealthyLiving #MobilityMatters #FootHealth

brand: Dr. Leada Malek, PT, DPT, SCS with Orthofeet
body: 10+ hours in bad shoes sucks. @orthofeet_us 👀 If you’re in healthcare, teaching, retail, hospitality, anything where you’re on your feet for 8-12+ hours straight, you KNOW the struggle. Half your day isn’t even over and your dogs are already barkin lmao. Nobody warns you in PT school that one of the hardest parts of the job would be your SHOES. 10 years in and so much time in khakis, a polo, and rotating between 2 pairs of pants that could survive exercise demos AND manual therapy AND still look somewhat professional. You could reach for sneakers but did not make you feel great by the end of the day. You just wore what everyone wore. They were an afterthought or whatever survived. Orthofeet happened and I genuinely don’t know why it took a decade. 12 hour standing days. walking, pivoting, crouching down to spot someone’s squat, back up, demoing more exercises. Hour 10 hits and my feet feel surprisingly... great. I used to feel like my feet were dead the thought of continuing on for a workout was tiring. A few people already asked what makes these different so here are my fave specs: -Adjustable arch support (!!) -Comfy insoles that cradle your feet and accommodate natural foot changes throughout the day -Wide toe box -Lightweight, breathable stretch upper -Pressure-free comfort contours to your foot shape, keeping sensitive areas like bunions and swollen feet free from irritation -60-day return policy so you can actually see if they can handle your life for 2 months! If you’ve been looking for a shoe to hold up for multiple active occasions and long hours, get a pair and try @orthofeet_us —- #orthofeetpartner #ad

3 jobs. 1 pair of shoes. 👟 Physical therapist 🩺, gym girl 🏋️‍♀️, marathon runner 🏃‍♀️… my feet genuinely don’t know the difference some days. As a PT, patients always ask me what shoes they should be wearing, and @orthofeet_us has become the one I actually tell them 💕. Real arch support, holds up through literally everything I throw at it ✨ Shop the pair in my bio 🔗 #orthofeetpartner

#AD Caregiver hooves deserve love, too. 🐴😂 Between chemotherapy appointments, therapies, hospital visits, and chasing a toddler who apparently has unlimited energy, my feet have been putting in some SERIOUS overtime. And while I'm pretty good at making sure Everly has everything she needs, taking care of myself? Ehhh, we're working on it. 🫠 So when I reached out to @orthofeet_us , I figured it was time to give the feet behind Everly's Entourage a little attention. 👟💜 Because you can't pour from an empty cup… or run on exhausted hooves. 😂 Thank you, @orthofeet_us , for gifting me these shoes and reminding this caregiver that she deserves a little TLC, too! #Orthofeet #CaregiverLife #MedicallyComplexMotherhood #EverlysEntourage #endnf

body: What if your knee pain isn't actually about your knee? What if it's about where the force is going? title: Neuropathy Pain? Start Here!
body: Living with diabetes and neuropathy meant my feet were extra sensitive. By the end of the day, I’d peel my socks off and see those deep red rings around my calves. My feet would feel hot, tender, and irritated, and the seams near my toes always seemed to rub in exactly the wrong place. When you have diabetes or neuropathy, little things don’t feel little. A tight band, a rough seam, or a thin sole can make the whole day harder. Then I tried Viasox EasyStretch™ Socks. The first thing I noticed was how easy they were to put on. No tugging. No fighting to get them over swollen feet. They stretched without squeezing, and the non-binding top actually stayed up without digging into my legs. Then I felt the cushioning. The triple-padded heel and toe gave my feet the softness regular socks never did. And the seamless toe? No rubbing. No irritation. Just smooth comfort. Now I can wear socks all day without constantly thinking about my feet. No deep marks. No tight elastic. No painful seams. Just soft, breathable comfort that finally feels made for sensitive, diabetic, and neuropathy-prone feet. If diabetes or neuropathy has made regular socks unbearable, Viasox EasyStretch™ Socks are worth trying.
